summary.value: The paper motivates that a new collaborative radiology reporting paradigm is required, as clinician oversight is an any case still required for AI-generated reports. They define “Report Collaboration Levels” in the current literature, arguing current works fall in level 1 and 2, which do not allow interactive/bidirectional collaboration. They propose a collaborative approach, where AI and radiologist interact on a “Anatomy-Finding-Contept Unit”, which they propose as a tuple of anatomy and finding, which they extract using DeepSeek, followed by semantic clustering using Sentence Transformer embeddings. They propose the “Concept Risk Score” as a metric to detect which of their concepts are too stable or not stable enough and therefore likely wrong and the “Holistic Semantic Match Metric” as a new report generation metric measuring IoU over the concepts they defined combined with cosine similarity of findings. The results show one round of correction improves the report generation result.

strengths.value:
- Interaction on an abstracted level seems promising for reducing interaction overhead  
- Minimal physician action leads to notable gains in performance on report generation  
- Rating error risk and deciding accordingly what to let the clinician correct makes sense and can reduce workload and the proposed uncertainty score seems to work better than other methods

weaknesses.value:
- Contribution claims: The five-fold contribution is over-claimed. I would say the main novelty lies in the concept-level interaction together with the uncertainty estimation \- the finetuning, and the metric as well as improved results should not be listed as unique contributions  
- Clarity:  
  - The authors define a lot of new names for rather simple concepts, making the paper hard to follow and overstating the contribution  
  - Figures 2 and 3 are very unclear  
  - Its not clear what table 1 shows and the results are not discussed in the result section, only shortly in the introduction  
- Method:  
  - The collaborative process is not really explained in the methodology, even though this is the main promise of the paper  
  - It's unclear if the fine-tuning process described in section 3.2 is needed. It seems like today's LLMs would be able to adapt a report given a flagged error without fine-tuning  
  - It seems like the only “interaction” is once correcting one finding that their risk score is classified as most probably wrong. That does not solve the problem of radiologists needing to double-check reports because there remains a lot of unchecked content in the report nevertheless. Why not allow correcting more than one finding if more findings are uncertain?  
- Results:  
  - It's unclear how the results of the proposed method are collected \- is a radiologist   
  - It is not surprising that performance improves when correcting mistakes. The method is only compared to one pass report generation methods without correction \- this does not really show that the proposed way of interaction is better than other interaction modes. A comparison of basic interaction modes in both time it takes as well as reached accuracy (judged by an external reader instead of an arbitrarily defined score) would be needed in my opinion  
  - It’s not clear why a new report generation metric is needed as opposed to using a similar concept as e.g. proposed in GreenScore.  
  - It’s unclear how the method was evaluated / how the interaction was simulated to get the corrected report.

questions.value:
- Why are finding concepts “clinically discriminative”? Also there ambiguity exists, e.g. “enlarged heart” vs “cardiomegaly”  
- How is the theoretical upper bound determined? Why is it not 1 for a fully correct report?

We appreciate your constructive comments and suggestions. We remain at your disposal for any additional clarifications.

**Q1:Overstated claims of contribution**

**R1:** We have revised the contribution statement and now organize it into three main contributions (see Line 99-107  for details): (i) We propose, for the first time, a bidirectional collaborative MRG framework, offering a novel perspective focused on trustworthiness and reducing physicians’ workload—a specific viewpoint not previously explored in the literature. (ii) We clarify why concept-level interaction serves as the most precise atomic language for human-AI collaboration, detailing how such concepts are extracted and leveraged in a fine-tuning strategy to enable vision-language models (VLMs) to understand physicians’ instructions and generate refined reports accordingly.(iii) We introduce CRS, an uncertainty estimation method grounded in VLM behavior.

The proposal of new metrics and performance improvements are regarded as supplementary contributions that provide fresh insights for medical report generation.

**Q2: Define a lot of new names.**

**R2:** In fact, we primarily define anatomical concepts and ​finding concepts​, and we have added a new section (Appendix A.19, Line 1572-1605) to explain the motivation and necessity behind these novel definitions.

Moreover, we have revised most parts of the manuscript that could cause ambiguity and highlighted these changes to further improve readability.

**Q3: Figures 2 and 3 are very unclear.**

**R3:** For Figure 2, we have added a new section (Appendix A.19, Line 1593-1605) to discuss it in detail.  Both report-level and sentence-level inputs are too coarse-grained for interactive correction. In clinical practice, radiologists rarely need to revise an entire sentence or full report; errors are typically localized—minor omissions or inaccuracies in specific descriptions. On the other hand, phrase-level segments (split by commas) often lack semantic completeness and are thus unsuitable. GPT concepts, while useful, tend to describe attributes in a weakly anchored manner—for example, “hyperechoic nodule” without clearly specifying which lobe (left or right), leading to ambiguity. In contrast, our AFCU framework explicitly separates: the anatomical concept (e.g., “right lobe”), and the finding concept (e.g., “hyperechoic nodule”). Only their combination yields a clear, unambiguous, atomic-level description. This design is fine-grained—enabling efficient human–AI interaction—and strongly anchored to specific anatomical locations, eliminating ambiguity.

For Figure 3, we have added explanatory text describing the three steps (Line 185-189) : (1) A fine-tuned VLM generates an initial report; (2) CRS identifies the anatomical concept with the highest error risk, and a physician provides the corrected description; (3) The VLM incorporates this feedback to produce the final revised report. And we also provide an English-only version of the image to improve readability (Figure 15).

**R8:** We collect results using a simulation-based approach. **Q11: It’s unclear how the method was evaluated / how the interaction was simulated to get the corrected report.**

**R11:** First, Figure 3 (Line 229-247) illustrates the overall pipeline. To improve readability, we provide a fully English version of the figure along with the procedural description in Line Figure 15 (Line 1429-1447).

Second, our simulation relies on a pre-constructed dictionary that maps each ground-truth report to its anatomical concepts and corresponding finding concepts. After generating a report, we use this dictionary to extract the anatomical and finding concepts from the generated text. CRS then estimates the uncertainty of each anatomical concept, and the (simulated) radiologist provides the corrected finding concept associated with the highest-risk anatomical concept. A concrete example is shown in Figure 3.

**Q12: Why are finding concepts “clinically discriminative”?**

**R12:** Finding concepts are determined by the perceptual similarity threshold described in Line 190-229, which is controlled—and, when necessary, manually refined—by researchers with medical expertise. Therefore, the "clinically discriminative" nature of these concepts depends on both the concept extraction process and the medical knowledge and judgment of the annotators.

**Q13: How is the theoretical upper bound determined? Why is it not 1 for a fully correct report?**

**R13:** First, UB denotes the theoretical upper bound under Concept Instruction Fine-tuning with intervention—specifically, the result obtained by feeding the complete ground-truth report as a prompt into the SFT-ed VLM. We have added this clarification in Appendix A.19, Line 1587-1592.

Second, in Appendix A.19, Line 1587-1592, we explain why providing the full ground-truth report as input to the VLM does not exactly reproduce the original report: this is because VLMs exhibit inherent stochasticity—even with identical input prompts, their outputs can vary due to random sampling during generation.

Thank you for your extensive rebuttal. While I still think the paper lacks overall in clarity, I appreciate the additional descriptions in regard to Q3, Q4, Q5 and Q8. I also appreciate the additional results provided regarding Q7 (correcting multiple findings), they add value to the paper.

Regarding Q6 and Q9, I think you have miss-understood my main concern. For both these new ablations, it seems VLMs that are not trained on on the US dataset are now given as comparison - as they will have a bad result already for the initial report, their bad metrics after correction are not surprising. My main question is indeed only about the correction part. A fitting ablation for this would e.g. be to use the report of a US-fine-tuned model e.g. Qwen 3b SFT from Table 2 and give this report together with a correction prompt to a zero-shot LLM e.g. again Qwen (as the fine-tuned model probably lost conversational abilities during fine-tuning) and report the results of the corrected report. It would be interesting to see this for both a "trivial" correction prompt, e.g. using full sentences and the proposed concept-level interaction. This form of basic VLM/LLM correction has also been proposed before e.g. in [1], so the claim that this does not exist is not correct. 

[1] Pellegrini, C., Özsoy, E., Busam, B., Wiestler, B., Navab, N., & Keicher, M. (2025). Radialog: Large vision-language models for x-ray reporting and dialog-driven assistance. In Medical Imaging with Deep Learning.

Regarding contibution, I think the contribution is still overclaimed. I remain with my opinion that there is one main contribution, which is the concept-level interaction *in combination* with the uncertainty estimation with the main result being the better selection of risk findings compared to e.g. random correction (Table 3). If the method proves to be significantly better in correcting based on the proposed AFCUs in above described experiments, this would also be a relevant result. Therefore it is not enough in my opinion to slighly rewrite the contribution paragraph, but instead the whole paper would need to be reframed both in terms of contribution and overall clarity.

For these reasons, my recommendation to reject the paper in its current form remains.

**Q2: Overclaimed contribution.**

**R2:** We have now added experiments (Appendix A.21) that demonstrate the effectiveness of our correction approach. As you noted, such a result would constitute a meaningful contribution, which our experiments now substantiate.

Moreover, our approach is not merely a correction method (like Radialog[1] you have cited). Instead, it actively evaluates the local uncertainty of the text generated by the Vision-Language Model and specifically instructs physicians to revise only the corresponding localized segments of the report. This is fundamentally different from Radialog, which requires physicians to comprehensively review the entire medical report alongside the full medical image. In our method, physicians examine only specific local image regions and their associated textual descriptions—guided by the VLM’s assessment of uncertainty regarding the descriptions of different anatomical structures. This represents a more advanced paradigm than RaDialog. In fact, we clearly define the three RCL levels in Figure 1 and Line 48-57 of the Introduction, where Radialog falls under RCL-1, while our work presents the first RCL-3 framework.

To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has explored this interaction mode. Accordingly, our concept-level investigations—centered on defining and formalizing this novel paradigm—constitute unique contributions of our work. Moreover, we do not believe that articulating multiple contributions necessarily amounts to overclaiming. Rather, we aim to clearly articulate how we progressively understood the problem and developed corresponding solutions, and we hope that summarizing the key methodological insights gained through our exploration will provide meaningful inspiration to readers.

Best regards,

Authors

summary.value: This paper presents a bidirectional collaborative framework for medical report generation that enhances model trustworthiness while reducing physicians’ workload. It leverages information bottleneck theory for concept-level feedback refinement and introduces the Concept Risk Score to prioritize high-impact diagnostic corrections. Additionally, it establishes concept-grounded semantic metrics and demonstrates a 9.13% improvement in report quality with minimal physician intervention.

strengths.value:
- The move to concept-level feedback refinement is original and relevant for real-world applications.
- The use of semantic similarity to go beyond simple overlap metrics is well motivated and adds depth. Also comparison with other metrics is beneficial. 
- The correlation analysis between the proposed metrics and human judgments / LLM evaluations is a strong plus and a meaningful evaluation.
- Report a quantifiable improvement (9.13%).

* The authors claim a five-fold contribution, but the paper really delivers two main contributions: the bidirectional collaborative interaction, uncertainty estimation and maybe the new metric.  
* Authors redefine existing definitions, making it hard to read the paper and confusing.  
* The presentation is uneven: mixing languages in figures, and a methodology section that interleaves high‐level design with implementation details and discussions, hurts readability.  
* It would be nice to see the proper evaluation of each part of the method, to understand where exactly the contribution is and what helped to improve the performance.   
* The paper has to be rewritten.  
* There are some interesting results in the tables, but they are not properly discussed or explained.

questions.value:
If the metric goes as a contribution, it would be worth comparing it to other semantic metrics like RaTEScore, GreenScore, GEMA‑Score and etc.

The authors introduce a collaborative interaction mechanism, yet they do not compare it to other methods under the same setup. Since giving one method the possibility to correct its mistakes makes it obvious that it will perform better, the more meaningful question is: if other competing methods were given the same correction-capability setup, would the proposed method still outperform them?

summary.value: This paper proposes a new medical report generation framework, RCL-3 (Report Collaboration Level-3), which aims to improve report credibility and reduce physician burden through a bidirectional collaboration mechanism between physicians and AI. The core concept is that AI first generates a draft report, then automatically detects and labels high-risk misconceptions. Physicians then manually correct only these "Anatomy-Finding Concept Units" (AFCUs). Finally, the AI regenerates the report based on the feedback. The paper's main modules include: AFCU concept extraction, which extracts anatomy and finding concepts from reports using DeepSeek-V3; Information Bottleneck Clustering, which merges semantically similar concepts to reduce redundancy; Concept Risk Score (CRS), which calculates visual-semantic instability through occlusion perturbation to prioritize physician intervention; and the Holistic Semantic Match (HSM) metric, which measures the semantic consistency between model output and human annotations. The paper reports an average HSM improvement of approximately 9.13% on four organ datasets (thyroid, breast, liver, and ovary), and claims that the report quality can be significantly improved by modifying only one AFCU.

strengths.value: This study offers a new perspective by framing report generation as a human-machine collaborative problem rather than a purely generative task. The main strength of this paper lies in its directional insights and conceptually valuable attempt to shift medical report generation from one-off automation to collaborative AI design. The proposed AFCU granularity is intuitive and reasonable, providing a middle ground between sentence-level and token-level semantics. Multi-organ experiments also demonstrate some generalization capabilities.

weaknesses.value:
1. Validation relies solely on machine-translated English datasets (from Chinese), risking distortion of nuanced clinical semantics; no tests on native English datasets (e.g., MIMIC-CXR) leave adaptability to English workflows uncertain.
2. The Concept Risk Score only detects high-risk concepts the model generates (e.g., incorrect nodules) but misses omitted critical concepts (e.g., unmentioned pleural effusions), limiting report safety.
3. The "single AFCU intervention" design lacks exploration of 2–3 high-risk AFCU corrections (for better efficiency-accuracy balance) and no discussion of low-risk error accumulation in practice.

questions.value:
1. How is bidirectional collaboration actually realized? Did any physicians participate in providing real feedback, or is it fully simulated?
2. How does the proposed CRS compare quantitatively with standard uncertainty estimation methods (entropy, ensemble variance, semantic entropy, etc.)?
3. What criteria were used to set the Information Bottleneck coefficient β? How sensitive are the results to this hyperparameter?
4. How stable is the correlation between HSM and established metrics (BLEU, CheXbert, RadGraph-F1) across datasets or random seeds?
5. The paper assumes that “correcting one AFCU” suffices—how realistic is this in multi-pathology cases where multiple findings coexist?
6. Would the framework still function effectively if the base model (e.g., LLaVA, Gemini, or Qwen) were replaced?
7. Has the study quantified the physician interaction cost or time savings through any real or simulated user experiments?

We deeply appreciate your time and effort dedicated to the review process. To support the newly assigned Area Chair and help streamline their evaluation process, we provide below a concise summary of the key points from the reviews and our responses.

Reviewer `yPVd` upgraded our score from 2 to 4 on November 26, 2025, at 18:42:18. Their remaining concerns primarily focus on (i) the collaborative interaction mechanism, (ii) Generalizability of the method and (iii) the clarity of the paper.

`Regarding (i)`, we have added Appendix A.21, which demonstrates that the core of our collaborative interaction mechanism lies in its fine-grained, strongly anchored binding of textual descriptions to specific anatomical structures—outperforming existing correction approaches.

`In terms of (ii)`, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across four anatomical organs using Qwen-VL-3B, Qwen-VL-7B, and MedGemma-4B, as shown in Table 2 (Lines 380–416) and the newly added experimental results (Lines 1242–1250), highlighting the broad applicability of our method.

`For (iii)`, we have added a clear description of the human–AI collaboration workflow in Lines 185–188 of the Method section and provided a fully English version of this workflow in Appendix A.17. Moreover, we have included extensive supplementary materials (Appendices A.13–A.21) to clarify any potentially ambiguous points. Notably, reviewers tMhq, SJet, and TNks all explicitly stated in their initial reviews that our paper features a clear and easy-to-follow presentation.

**2. Reviewer `kJoU`**

In their response dated November 25, 2025, at 18:26:40, Reviewer `kJoU` acknowledged parts of our rebuttal and recognized that the newly added content adds value to the paper. Regarding their lingering concerns about Q6 and Q9, `kJoU suggested conducting a new experiment` to verify whether our AFCU-based correction outperforms Radialog specifically in the correction phase, noting that “this would also be a relevant result” if proven true. `We strictly followed this suggestion and added the new experiment` in Appendix A.21, which clearly shows that our AFCU method surpasses Radialog in correction effectiveness—thus resolving this concern.

Regarding kJoU’s other concern—that `our contribution is still overclaimed, and that our work could only be reduced to uncertainty estimation unless we demonstrated AFCU’s superiority in correction`—`we have now provided exactly that evidence via Appendix A.21`. As kJoU themselves noted, such a result would constitute a meaningful contribution, which our experiments now substantiate.

More importantly, we explicitly define three Radiology Collaboration Levels (RCL) in Figure 1 and Lines 48–57 of the Introduction: Radialog falls under RCL-1 (one-way assistance), whereas our work presents the first RCL-3 framework (risk-aware, proactive collaboration). To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has explored this human–AI interaction paradigm. Therefore, our concept-level modeling and formalization of this novel framework constitute a unique contribution. Furthermore, we maintain that clearly articulating multiple contributions does not equate to overclaiming; rather, it reflects our progressive understanding of the problem and the corresponding solution design. We hope that summarizing these key methodological insights will offer meaningful inspiration to the community.

Reviewer `TNks` raised five specific issues: (i) improving readability affected by Chinese content; (ii) adding Clinical Efficacy (CE) metrics; (iii) including comparisons with recent methods; (iv) providing a theoretical analysis of CRS; (v) clarifying that relying on LLMs’ self-assessed uncertainty fails to reduce physician workload.We addressed `(i)`by adding Appendix A.17 (“Language Presentation and Accessibility”) with fully English versions of all figures.`For (ii) and (iii)`, we added Appendix A.15 (“Enhancing Clinical Efficacy on the English IU-Xray Dataset”), which includes CE metrics and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods (e.g., ICCV 2025, AAAI 2024). `For (iv)`, we added Appendix A.18 (“Theoretical Analysis of the Concept Risk Score”). `For (v)`, we clarified that our method does not rely on the LLM’s self-assessed uncertainty or reasoning capabilities; instead, we identify report segments at high risk of inaccuracy or inconsistency—regardless of the cause—using an objective, perturbation-based signal.

We have also fully addressed all questions from reviewers `tMhq` and `SJet`. Notably, our new Section 4.7 (“Impact of Multiple CRS Concept Injection”) demonstrates that our method remains effective even when correcting multiple localized errors simultaneously, highlighting its strong potential as a new paradigm for human–AI collaborative report generation.
